name: Treaty with the Winnebago, 1829 (Treaty of Prairie du Chien)
promises: Article 2: $18,000 in specie a year for thirty years, $30,000 in goods at once, and 3,000 pounds of tobacco and 50 barrels of salt a year for thirty years.
Article 3: three blacksmith shops for thirty years, two yoke of oxen, a cart and a hired man at the Fox-Wisconsin portage.
Article 4: payment of $23,532.28 to named creditors in full satisfaction of their claims against the Winnebago.
Article 5: land grants to named descendants of Winnebago people, located outside the mineral country.

breaches.what: The Winnebago claimed further payment for Royce Area 149 ceded by this treaty. The Commission found the area worth $2,025,000.00 on January 2, 1830 but never ruled on the price paid; the claim was settled by compromise together with two other dockets for $4,600,000.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Winnebago Tribe and Nation of Indians et al. v. United States, Dockets 243, 244 and 245, Findings of Fact on Compromise Settlement (September 3, 1970)

source.title: Winnebago Tribe and Nation of Indians et al. v. United States, Dockets 243-245, Findings of Fact on Compromise Settlement (September 3, 1970)
source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Library, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

compensation: On October 13, 1965 the Commission found the fair market value of Royce Area 149 was $2,025,000.00, or about $0.75 an acre, on January 2, 1830. The consideration paid was never determined; the Winnebago claims in Dockets 243, 244 and 245 were settled in 1970 for a net final judgment of $4,600,000.
today: The compromise was approved by the governing bodies of the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska and the Wisconsin Winnebago (now the Ho-Chunk Nation). A compromise is not a finding that the treaty was broken.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation says its oral tradition holds that the Ho-Chunk have always been here, and that its traditional lands run through Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri and Illinois.

openQuestions: The $4,600,000 settlement covers three dockets (243, 244, 245); the share for this treaty's cession is not stated.
The acreage of Royce Area 149 in the 1965 findings is OCR-damaged and was left out; confirm it against the scan.
No Ho-Chunk Nation or Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska account of this treaty specifically was found.

plain.promised: Thirty years of yearly payments, goods, tobacco and salt, three blacksmith shops, and payment of traders' claims, in return for the lead-mining country of northern Illinois and southern Wisconsin.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission valued the land at $2,025,000.00 in 1830 but never ruled on the price paid. The claim was settled by compromise in 1970.
plain.today: The settlement paid $4,600,000 for this and two other Winnebago claims together. A compromise is not a finding that the treaty was broken.
